kurals.tamil:
ஆற்று பவர்க்கும் அரண்பொருள் அஞ்சித்தற்
போற்று பவர்க்கும் பொருள்.
kurals.transliteration:
Aatru pavarkkum aranporul anjiththar
potru pavarkkum porul.
kurals.meaning: A fortress is a prized possession both for the king who marches out to attack and for the one who, fearing attack, shelters behind it to protect himself.
kurals.elementary: Think of a tree house with a strong ladder. When you want to go out and play a game of tag, it is your safe base to run out from. When it starts to rain or a big dog chases you, it is the place you run back into. Valluvar says a fort is useful in both ways, for going out and for staying safe.
kurals.university: The chapter opens the Kural’s treatment of aran (fortification), the last of the six angas (limbs) of the state listed in kural 381 (padai, kudi, koozh, amaichu, natpu, aran). The couplet is built on a balanced contrast: aatrupavar are ‘those who act’, which Parimelazhagar and the modern commentators (Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah, Kalaignar) take as those who go out to make war on others, while anjith than potrupavar are ‘those who, fearing, guard themselves’, the besieged who seek shelter. The word porul is used twice, first as ‘a thing of value’ (aran porul, ‘the fort is a treasure’) and then as the predicate, a deliberate play on the same word that also names the whole second book of the Kural (Porutpaal). The point is that a fortress is not merely defensive: it is a base of operations for offense and a refuge in weakness alike. The sandhi-joined text on thirukkural-thamizh.org reads ‘ஆற்று பவர்க்கு மரண்பொரு ளஞ்சித்தற்’, which divides into the same words as the ytamizh.com text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One bowman, placed on a rampart, is a match in battle for one hundred (foes), one hundred for ten thousand; hence it is prescribed (in the Sastras that a king will posses) a fortress.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu tells the king that a fort multiplies the strength of every defender, which is why the law books require a king to have one.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, Manu treats the fort as an essential royal asset because of the military advantage it gives.
hinduism.source: Manusmriti 7.74 (trans. G. Bühler, Sacred Books of the East vol. 25)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong match on the fort’s value; Manu stresses defensive multiplication rather than the Kural’s attack-and-refuge pairing. The spelling ‘posses’ is as printed in the online Bühler text.

christianity.quote_or_event: “When a strong man armed keepeth his palace, his goods are in peace.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus uses the image of an armed man guarding a stronghold to describe how security keeps what is inside safe.
christianity.tie_back: The image matches the Kural’s second half: a guarded stronghold is what keeps the fearful safe.
christianity._accuracy_note: Jesus is using a parable about spiritual power, not teaching statecraft; the parallel is to the image only.

islam.quote_or_event: “They said, ‘O Dhul-Qarnayn, indeed Gog and Magog are [great] corrupters in the land. So may we assign for you an expenditure that you might make between us and them a barrier?’”
islam.explanation: A people suffering from raiders offer to pay Dhul-Qarnayn to build them a protective barrier.
islam.tie_back: Their offer shows what the Kural says: to those who live in fear, a fortification is worth paying for.
islam._accuracy_note: Covers the defensive half of the couplet well but not the attacker’s use of a fort.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He acted with vigor, rebuilding the whole breached wall, raising towers on it, and building another wall outside it.”
judaism.explanation: When the Assyrian king Sennacherib came against Jerusalem, King Hezekiah’s first act was to repair and double the city walls.
judaism.tie_back: Hezekiah, threatened and afraid, turns to the fort as his chief asset, just as the Kural describes.
judaism._accuracy_note: Illustrates the defensive value of walls; the Kural’s claim that forts also serve attackers is not addressed.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “With this first requisite of a fortress it is well provided for the protection of those within and to ward off those without.”
buddhism.explanation: In the Nagara Sutta the Buddha lists the parts of a royal frontier fortress, repeating that each one both protects those inside and drives off those outside.
buddhism.tie_back: The refrain has the same two-sided use as the Kural: the fort serves both defense and active resistance.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 7.63, Nagara Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close structural parallel, though the sutta uses the fort as a simile for spiritual qualities.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad, Poseidon recalls that he and Apollo built the walls of Troy for King Laomedon, and those god-built walls sheltered the Trojans throughout the war while Hector used the city as a base for his attacks on the Greek camp.
greek_mythology.explanation: Troy’s walls served the Trojans both as a refuge when they were driven back and as the starting point for their sallies.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Troy shows both uses the Kural names: a base for those who attack and a shelter for those who defend.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased narrative; the dual use is drawn from the story, not stated as a teaching.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Those who have their cities surrounded by walls may either take advantage of them or not, but cities which are unwalled have no choice.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues against those who scorn walls: walls give a city options, while having none leaves it no choice at all.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle, like Valluvar, sees the fort as a resource that serves a city whether it attacks or defends.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong conceptual match on the fort as a flexible asset.

kurals.tamil:
மணிநீரும் மண்ணும் மலையும் அணிநிழற்
காடும் உடைய தரண்.
kurals.transliteration:
Maninheerum mannum malaiyum aninizhar
kaadum udaiya tharan.
kurals.meaning: A true fortress has water as clear as a gem, open ground, hills and a forest with thick shade.
kurals.elementary: Imagine building a pillow fort. It is best to put it behind the sofa, beside a blanket ‘river’, with a big armchair ‘mountain’ next to it and lots of cushions like a forest. Anyone sneaking up has to cross all of that first. Valluvar says the best forts use nature in the same way: water, open ground, hills and forest.
kurals.university: Here Valluvar lists the natural defenses (iyarkai aran) that should surround a fort: mani neer (water clear as a gem, i.e. a moat or lake that never dries), mann (land, glossed by Varadarasanar and Pappaiah as open ground with no cover for an attacker), malai (hill) and ani nizhal kaadu (forest of beautiful or dense shade). Parimelazhagar and the later commentators read these as four types of fort: neer aran, nila aran, malai aran and kaattu aran. Pappaiah states this directly. The list closely parallels the Sanskrit arthashastra classification into water-fort (audaka), mountain-fort (parvata), desert or open-land fort (dhanvana) and forest-fort (vanadurga), which suggests a shared South Asian military science that the next couplet calls simply ‘the treatise’ (nool). Kalaignar reads mani neer as a deep, wide moat. The sandhi-joined text reads ‘மணிநீரு மண்ணு மலையு மணிநிழற் / காடு முடைய தரண்’, which divides into the same words.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “a water-fortification (audaka) such as an island in the midst of a river, or a plain surrounded by low ground; a mountainous fortification (párvata) such as a rocky tract or a cave; a desert (dhánvana) such as a wild tract devoid of water and overgrown with thicket growing in barren soil; or a forest fortification (vanadurga) full of wagtail (khajana), water and thickets.”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya names four kinds of natural fortification to be built at the kingdom’s borders: water, mountain, desert and forest.
hinduism.tie_back: This is almost the same four-part list as the Kural’s water, land, hill and forest.
hinduism.source: Kautilya, Arthashastra 2.3 ‘Construction of Forts’ (trans. R. Shamasastry)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match of the four natural defenses; Kautilya’s ‘desert’ corresponds to the Kural’s open land.

christianity.quote_or_event: “He shall dwell on high: his place of defence shall be the munitions of rocks: bread shall be given him; his waters shall be sure.”
christianity.explanation: Isaiah promises the righteous a high rocky stronghold with guaranteed bread and water.
christianity.tie_back: Isaiah’s ideal refuge combines the height of hills with an assured water supply, two of the Kural’s natural defenses.
christianity._accuracy_note: Covers hill and water; forest and open land are absent, and the verse is a prophetic promise, not military advice.

islam.quote_or_event: “And Allah has made for you, from that which He has created, shadows and has made for you from the mountains, shelters.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an counts shade and mountain shelters among God’s gifts for human protection.
islam.tie_back: Shade and mountains are two of the natural protections the Kural wants around a fort.
islam._accuracy_note: The verse is about divine provision generally, not fortification; the overlap is in the natural features named.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A large force was assembled to stop up all the springs and the wadi that flowed through the land, for otherwise, they thought, the king of Assyria would come and find water in abundance.”
judaism.explanation: Before the Assyrian siege, Hezekiah’s men blocked the springs outside Jerusalem so that the besiegers would have no water.
judaism.tie_back: It shows the Kural’s point that controlling water is itself a fortification.
judaism._accuracy_note: Matches on water as a defensive resource only.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Furthermore, the royal frontier fortress has a moat, both deep & wide.”
buddhism.explanation: The second requisite of the Buddha’s model fortress is a deep, wide moat.
buddhism.tie_back: The moat is the Kural’s ‘gem-clear water’, the first natural defense on its list.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 7.63, Nagara Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Only the water element matches; the sutta’s moat is man-made rather than a natural feature.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Odyssey, the princess Nausicaa describes the city of the Phaeacians to Odysseus as surrounded by a high wall, with a fine harbour on either side and a narrow entrance, a site protected by the sea on both flanks.
greek_mythology.explanation: The ideal city of the Phaeacians is protected mainly by its natural setting of water and a narrow approach.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, Homer’s ideal city depends on natural surroundings as much as on its wall.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; only the water and narrow-approach features correspond to the Kural’s list.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “There should be a natural abundance of springs and fountains in the town, or, if there is a deficiency of them, great reservoirs may be established for the collection of rainwater, such as will not fail when the inhabitants are cut off from the country …”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle requires the ideal city’s site to have a water supply that cannot fail even during a war.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle, like Valluvar, begins good fortification with the natural site, and above all with water.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong on water; Aristotle does not list hill and forest as the Kural does. The quote is cut before the words ‘by war’.

kurals.tamil:
உயர்வகலம் திண்மை அருமைஇந் நான்கின்
அமைவரண் என்றுரைக்கும் நூல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Uyarvakalam thinmai arumaiin naankin
amaivaran endruraikkum nool.
kurals.meaning: The treatises say that a fort is a wall that has four qualities together: height, breadth, strength and inaccessibility.
kurals.elementary: A good sandcastle wall has to be tall so the waves can’t jump over it, thick so they can’t push through, packed hard so it doesn’t crumble, and hard to reach, maybe behind a ditch. If any one of these is missing, the sea gets in. Valluvar says the old books on forts ask for the same four things.
kurals.university: After the natural defenses (742), Valluvar turns to the man-made wall (seyarkai aran, as Pappaiah calls it) and gives its four standard qualities: uyarvu (height, so that it cannot be scaled), akalam (breadth, which Pappaiah explains as room for defenders to stand and move on the rampart), thinmai (solidity, so that it cannot be battered down) and arumai (difficulty or inaccessibility). Parimelazhagar’s tradition explains arumai as the difficulty of approach created by engines and traps (pori) set on the walls, a reading that Pappaiah follows. The phrase endru uraikkum nool, ‘so says the treatise’, is one of the places where Valluvar openly cites earlier military and political science. Commentators link it to the arthashastra tradition, whose fort specifications (for example, a rampart ‘six dandas high and twice as much broad’) are very similar. The sandhi-joined text reads ‘உயர்வகலந் திண்மை யருமையிந் நான்கி / னமைவர ணென்றுரைக்கு நூல்’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “a rampart six dandas high and twice as much broad shall be erected by heaping mud upwards and by making it square at the bottom, oval at the centre pressed by the trampling of elephants and bulls, and planted with thorny and poisonous plants in bushes.”
hinduism.explanation: The Arthashastra gives exact measurements for a fort’s rampart, packed hard by elephants and bulls and planted with thorny bushes.
hinduism.tie_back: It sets out the Kural’s four qualities: height, breadth, strength (packed earth) and inaccessibility (thorns).
hinduism.source: Kautilya, Arthashastra 2.3 ‘Construction of Forts’ (trans. R. Shamasastry)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close technical parallel and a likely example of the kind of ‘nool’ the Kural cites.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And had a wall great and high, and had twelve gates, and at the gates twelve angels.”
christianity.explanation: John’s vision of the New Jerusalem describes a great, high wall with gates guarded by angels.
christianity.tie_back: The ideal heavenly city has the Kural’s height and greatness, with guarded and hard-to-reach entrances.
christianity._accuracy_note: A symbolic vision, not a building specification; matches height, size and guarded access.

islam.quote_or_event: “Bring me sheets of iron” - until, when he had leveled [them] between the two mountain walls, he said, “Blow [with bellows],” until when he had made it [like] fire, he said, “Bring me, that I may pour over it molten copper.”
islam.explanation: Dhul-Qarnayn builds his barrier from iron fused with molten copper and fills the gap between two mountains with it.
islam.tie_back: The barrier is as high as the mountains and as solid as metal, showing the Kural’s height and strength.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong on height and solidity; breadth is not mentioned.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Walk around Zion, circle it; count its towers, take note of its ramparts; go through its citadels, that you may recount it to a future age.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist invites pilgrims to walk around Jerusalem and admire its towers and ramparts as a sign of God’s protection.
judaism.tie_back: The psalm praises the same features the Kural lists: tall towers and strong ramparts.
judaism.source: Psalms 48:13-14 (JPS Tanakh, Gender-Sensitive Edition 2023, via Sefaria; KJV 48:12-13)
judaism._accuracy_note: Praises fortifications but gives no technical criteria. The translation notes that the meaning of ‘go through’ is uncertain.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Furthermore, the royal frontier fortress has ramparts: high & thick & completely covered with plaster.”
buddhism.explanation: The seventh requisite of the Buddha’s fortress is a high, thick, fully plastered rampart.
buddhism.tie_back: High, thick and sealed is almost the Kural’s height, breadth and strength.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 7.63, Nagara Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close match on three of the four qualities.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Odyssey, Odysseus sees in the underworld Antiope’s twin sons Amphion and Zethus, who founded seven-gated Thebes and surrounded it with towers, because even with all their strength they could not live in wide Thebes without walls. Later tradition says Amphion’s lyre made the stones move into place by themselves.
greek_mythology.explanation: The founders of Thebes knew that even great strength needs a high, towered wall around it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s tall, strong wall is the same thing the mythic founders of Thebes thought a city could not do without.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; it supports the need for high walls in general, not the four specific qualities.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “not only should cities have walls, but care should be taken to make them ornamental, as well as useful for warlike purposes, and adapted to resist modern inventions.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle wants city walls that look fine but are above all built to resist the latest siege engines.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle’s wall ‘adapted to resist’ attack is the Kural’s idea of arumai: a wall made hard to overcome.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Matches the concern with strength against attack; Aristotle gives no fourfold list. A missing space in the online text has been restored.

kurals.tamil:
சிறுகாப்பிற் பேரிடத்த தாகி உறுபகை
ஊக்கம் அழிப்ப தரண்.
kurals.transliteration:
Sirukaappir peridaththa thaaki urupakai
ookkam azhippa tharan.
kurals.meaning: A fortress should have only a few points that need guarding but plenty of space inside, and it should break the spirit of any enemy that attacks it.
kurals.elementary: Think of a playground fort with just one small doorway and lots of room inside. You only need one friend at the door to keep watch, while everyone else can play inside. And anyone who tries to get in soon gives up, because the doorway is so hard to rush. That is Valluvar’s kind of fort.
kurals.university: The couplet sets two design principles against each other: siru kaappu (small guard-length, i.e. few places that need to be defended) and per idam (large interior space). The commentators all explain this as a narrow, easily held perimeter or entrance around a spacious interior; Kalaignar says that the part to be protected is small while the inside is wide. The second line gives the purpose: urupakai ookkam azhippathu, ‘that which destroys the zeal of the strong enemy who comes against it’. Pappaiah glosses this as filling the besiegers with dismay. The idea is psychological as much as structural: a well-designed fort defeats the attacker’s morale before it defeats his army. Parimelazhagar treats the chapter’s verses from 743 on as a list of the defining marks (ilakkanam) of a man-made fort. The sandhi-joined text reads ‘சிறுகாப்பிற் பேரிடத்த தாகி யுறுபகை / யூக்க மழிப்ப தரண்’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Let him cause to be built for himself, in the centre of it, a spacious palace, (well) protected, habitable in every season, resplendent (with whitewash), supplied with water and trees.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu tells the king to build a spacious, well-protected palace at the centre of his fort.
hinduism.tie_back: A roomy interior inside a guarded ring is the Kural’s ‘ample within, small to guard’.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Matches the spacious interior; says nothing about breaking the enemy’s morale.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs describes God as a tower that anyone righteous can run into and be safe.
christianity.tie_back: A single strong tower with room for all who shelter there echoes the Kural’s small-to-guard, large-within fort.
christianity._accuracy_note: A spiritual metaphor with only a loose structural parallel.

islam.quote_or_event: “So Gog and Magog were unable to pass over it, nor were they able [to effect] in it any penetration.”
islam.explanation: Once Dhul-Qarnayn’s barrier closed the single gap between the mountains, the raiders could neither climb it nor break through.
islam.tie_back: One narrow gap sealed between natural walls stops a whole hostile people: few points to guard, and an enemy’s drive brought to nothing.
islam._accuracy_note: Good match on a narrow sealed gap that defeats attackers; interior space is not mentioned.

judaism.quote_or_event: “There is much work and it is spread out; we are scattered over the wall, far from one another. When you hear a trumpet call, gather yourselves to me at that place; our God will fight for us!”
judaism.explanation: Nehemiah, rebuilding Jerusalem’s wall with too few men, sets up a trumpet signal so that the defenders can gather at whatever point is attacked.
judaism.tie_back: Nehemiah faces the very problem the Kural solves: a long wall needs a small number of points that must actually be guarded.
judaism.source: Nehemiah 4:13-14 (JPS Tanakh, Gender-Sensitive Edition 2023, via Sefaria; KJV 4:19-20)
judaism._accuracy_note: Shows the problem of a long perimeter; the Kural states the design ideal instead.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as a border city is closely guarded both within and without, even so, guard yourself.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells his followers to guard themselves as carefully as a frontier city is guarded.
buddhism.tie_back: The closely guarded border city is the Kural’s fort, where careful guarding makes the whole place secure.
buddhism._accuracy_note: A general image of vigilant guarding, used as a simile for self-discipline.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Herodotus describes the pass of Thermopylae as a narrow way between the mountains and the sea, where the Greeks rebuilt an old wall. There Leonidas and a small Greek force held back Xerxes’ huge army for several days, and even the Persian king’s elite Immortals were driven back.
greek_mythology.explanation: A narrow front let a few defenders hold off many attackers and badly damage their confidence.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Thermopylae is a real example of the Kural’s narrow point to guard that ‘destroys the enemy’s zeal’.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Historical rather than mythological, and a pass rather than a fort, but the principle matches closely.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The general, unable to control his irritation, will launch his men to the assault like swarming ants, with the result that one-third of his men are slain, while the town still remains untaken.”
philosophy.explanation: Sun Tzu warns that besieging a well-walled town makes the attacking general reckless and wastes his army.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s point seen from the attacker’s side: a good fort wears down the enemy’s spirit as well as his army.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War 3.5 (trans. Lionel Giles)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong match on the fort breaking the besieger’s morale.

kurals.tamil:
கொளற்கரிதாய்க் கொண்டகூழ்த் தாகி அகத்தார்
நிலைக்கெளிதாம் நீரது அரண்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kolarkarithaaik kondakoozhth thaaki akaththaar
nilaikkelithaam neerathu aran.
kurals.meaning: A fortress should be hard to capture, well stocked with food, and easy for the people inside to hold and fight from.
kurals.elementary: If you are playing a long game of capture-the-flag, your base needs three things. It should be hard for the other team to get into, it should have snacks and water so you don’t have to leave, and it should be easy for your own team to move around in. Valluvar says a real fort needs the same three things.
kurals.university: The couplet names three conditions. Kolarku arithaai means ‘hard to take’; Pappaiah adds ‘even under a siege of many days’. Konda koozhthu aagi means ‘holding provisions’. Koozh (literally gruel or food) is the same word that names the Koozhiyal (the section on wealth and resources) in some divisions of the Porutpaal, and here it means stored food. Akaththaar nilaikku elithaam means ‘easy for those within to hold their position’. Varadarasanar reads this as easy for the defenders to stay in, while Pappaiah and Kalaignar read it as convenient for the defenders to fight from. The final neerathu (‘of such a nature’) marks the three conditions as the fort’s defining nature. The ytamizh text reads ‘நிலைக்கெளிதாம் நீரது’, and the sandhi-joined text on thirukkural-thamizh.org reads ‘நிலைக்கெளிதா நீர தரண்’. These are orthographic variants of the same words.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Let that (fort) be well supplied with weapons, money, grain and beasts of burden, with Brahmanas, with artisans, with engines, with fodder, and with water.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu lists everything a royal fort must hold, from grain and water to weapons and skilled people.
hinduism.tie_back: Manu’s well-supplied fort is exactly the Kural’s fort ‘holding provisions’.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus says that anyone planning to build a tower must first make sure he has the resources to finish it.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats a stronghold as useless without enough resources behind it.
christianity._accuracy_note: A parable about counting the cost of discipleship; the link is to planning resources, not to storing food for a siege.

islam.quote_or_event: “[Joseph] said, ‘You will plant for seven years consecutively; and what you harvest leave in its spikes, except a little from which you will eat.’”
islam.explanation: Joseph advises Egypt to store most of seven years’ harvest in preparation for the famine to come.
islam.tie_back: Stored grain against hard times is the Kural’s ‘konda koozh’, the fort’s food reserve.
islam._accuracy_note: Provisioning against famine, not siege; the parallel is limited to storing food.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He strengthened the fortified towns and put commanders in them, along with stores of food, oil, and wine, and shields and spears in every town.”
judaism.explanation: King Rehoboam fortified the towns of Judah and stocked each one with food, oil, wine and weapons.
judaism.tie_back: A strong fort stocked with food is exactly what this couplet asks for.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close match on a strengthened and provisioned fort.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Furthermore, it has large stores of rice & barley for the delight, convenience, & comfort of those within, and to ward off those without.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha’s ideal fortress keeps large grain stores so that those inside are comfortable and can resist those outside.
buddhism.tie_back: This joins the Kural’s ideas of stored food and a fort that is ‘easy for those within’.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 7.63, Nagara Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close match on provisions and ease for the defenders.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Herodotus reports that when Cyrus besieged Babylon, the Babylonians had stored provisions for many years in advance and did not worry about the siege. Cyrus took the city only by diverting the Euphrates and entering along the riverbed.
greek_mythology.explanation: Babylon’s stores made it almost impossible to starve out, so the attacker had to use a trick instead.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Babylon illustrates the Kural’s provisioned fort and hints at its warning, in the next couplets, about stratagem.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Historical narrative, not myth. It matches on provisions, but the city did fall.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “With a view to the latter it should afford easy egress to the citizens, and at the same time be inaccessible and difficult of capture to enemies.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says that, for war, a city’s site should make movement easy for its own citizens and approach hard for enemies.
philosophy.tie_back: This is almost word for word the Kural’s ‘hard to capture’ yet ‘easy for those within’.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on two of the three conditions; provisions are covered elsewhere in the same chapter.

kurals.tamil:
எல்லாப் பொருளும் உடைத்தாய் இடத்துதவும்
நல்லாள் உடையது அரண்.
kurals.transliteration:
Ellaap porulum udaiththaai idaththuthavum
nallaal udaiyathu aran.
kurals.meaning: A true fortress holds everything that might be needed and has brave, good men who will help when danger comes.
kurals.elementary: A good school on a stormy day has torches, blankets and food in the cupboard. But it also needs calm grown-ups who know what to do when the lights go out. Supplies alone are not enough; you need good people too. Valluvar says the same about a fort.
kurals.university: The first line (ellaap porulum udaiththaai, ‘having all things’) sums up the material requirements of 745, and the second line brings in the human element that the chapter’s last couplet will make decisive: idaththu uthavum nallaal, ‘good men who help at the (critical) place or time’. Idam can mean both the spot where danger arises and the moment of need, and Varadarasanar reads it as the moment of crisis in battle. Nallaal (nal + aal, ‘good person’) is read by all the commentators as brave warriors: Pappaiah speaks of heroes who can defeat enemies trying to destroy the fort from outside, and Kalaignar of strong fighters who leap into battle. The pairing of stores and soldiers reflects the arthashastra and Dharmashastra habit of listing a fort’s supplies and its garrison together. The sandhi-joined text reads ‘எல்லாப் பொருளு முடைத்தா யிடத்துதவு / நல்லா ளுடைய தரண்’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Let him build (there) a town, making for his safety a fortress, protected by a desert, or a fortress built of (stone and) earth, or one protected by water or trees, or one (formed by an encampment of armed) men or a hill-fort.”
hinduism.explanation: Among the six kinds of fort, Manu includes one made of nothing but armed men (the nri-durga).
hinduism.tie_back: Manu treats good fighting men as a fortress in their own right, which is the Kural’s point about ‘good men who help’.
hinduism._accuracy_note: The ‘fort of men’ matches the human element; Manu gives this as a separate type, not as part of every fort.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Or what king, going to make war against another king, sitteth not down first, and consulteth whether he be able with ten thousand to meet him that cometh against him with twenty thousand?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus says a wise king counts his soldiers before going to war.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats having enough capable fighters as basic to military success.
christianity._accuracy_note: A parable about discipleship; only the concern with enough troops carries over.

islam.quote_or_event: “And prepare against them whatever you are able of power and of steeds of war by which you may terrify the enemy of Allah and your enemy.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an tells the believers to prepare every kind of strength and cavalry they can to deter their enemies.
islam.tie_back: Being ready with ‘whatever you are able of power’ matches the Kural’s fort that has all things and able men.
islam._accuracy_note: Close on general readiness; not specifically about fortification.

judaism.quote_or_event: “From that day on, half my servants did work and half held lances and shields, bows and armor.”
judaism.explanation: While Jerusalem’s wall was being rebuilt, Nehemiah kept half his men armed and on guard.
judaism.tie_back: A wall needs armed men ready to defend it, which is the Kural’s ‘good men who help in need’.
judaism.source: Nehemiah 4:10 (JPS Tanakh, Gender-Sensitive Edition 2023, via Sefaria; KJV 4:16)
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong on the human element; supplies are not in view.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Furthermore, the royal frontier fortress has a large army stationed within — elephant soldiers, cavalry, charioteers, bowmen, standard-bearers, billeting officers, soldiers of the supply corps, noted princes, commando heroes, infantry, & slaves.”
buddhism.explanation: The fifth requisite of the Buddha’s fortress is a full garrison of every kind of soldier stationed inside.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s ‘nallaal’, the fighters who make the stored fort useful.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 7.63, Nagara Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close match; the sutta separately lists the stores, just as the Kural pairs the two.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aeschylus’ Seven Against Thebes, as seven enemy champions prepare to storm the seven gates of Thebes, King Eteocles chooses a matching Theban champion to hold each gate, himself taking the seventh.
greek_mythology.explanation: The safety of Thebes depends on posting a fit defender at every gate.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The walls of Thebes are only as good as the men who help at each point of danger, which is the Kural’s ‘idaththu uthavum nallaal’.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; a close dramatic example of defenders placed where they are needed.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “for when men are well prepared no enemy even thinks of attacking them.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle ends his discussion of city defenses by saying that good preparation discourages attack in the first place.
philosophy.tie_back: A fort fully stocked and well manned, as the Kural requires, is one that enemies do not dare to attack.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Matches the purpose of readiness; not specific about supplies and men.

kurals.tamil:
முற்றியும் முற்றா தெறிந்தும் அறைப்படுத்தும்
பற்றற் கரியது அரண்.
kurals.transliteration:
Mutriyum mutraa therindhum araippaduththum
patrar kariyathu aran.
kurals.meaning: A true fortress cannot be taken by blockade, by direct assault without a blockade, or by treachery from within.
kurals.elementary: Imagine your best toy locked in a treasure box. Someone might wait outside your room for hours, or try to grab it quickly, or even trick your little brother into opening the box. A really safe box beats all three tricks. Valluvar says a real fort must be safe from waiting, grabbing and tricking.
kurals.university: The couplet lists the three ways a fort can be taken and says a true aran resists all of them: mutriyum (by besieging it all round), mutraathu erindhum (by attacking without a full siege, i.e. storming a weak point), and araippaduththum (by araippadal, which Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read as vanjanai, deceit or treachery, and Pappaiah as turning some of those inside into a fifth column). Pope’s English (‘mine beneath the ground’) follows the other old sense of arai as a hollow or underground passage, so there is a real divergence between treachery and undermining; the Tamil commentarial tradition generally prefers treachery. The sandhi-joined text reads ‘முற்றியு முற்றா தெறிந்து மறைப்படுத்தும்’, where ‘எறிந்து மறைப்படுத்தும்’ is the sandhi form of ‘எறிந்தும் அறைப்படுத்தும்’, which confirms the reading araippaduththum. The inclusion of treachery points ahead to 750: the human element can undo even a physically perfect fort.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Book XIII of the Arthashastra, titled Strategic Means to Capture a Fortress, teaches a conqueror to take forts by sowing dissension among the defenders, using spies and secret agents inside the walls, and only then by siege and assault.
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya treats subversion from inside as just as important as siege and storm in taking a fort.
hinduism.tie_back: The same three methods (siege, assault and inside treachery) are what the Kural’s fort must resist.
hinduism.source: Kautilya, Arthashastra, Book XIII (trans. R. Shamasastry)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased summary of the book’s scope, not verified against the text line by line.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But when a stronger than he shall come upon him, and overcome him, he taketh from him all his armour wherein he trusted, and divideth his spoils.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus continues his image: an armed man’s stronghold is safe only until someone stronger overpowers it.
christianity.tie_back: It warns of what the Kural’s fort must prevent: being taken by a stronger assault.
christianity._accuracy_note: Spiritual parable; it shows the danger without the Kural’s three methods of capture.

islam.quote_or_event: “they thought that their fortresses would protect them from Allah; but [the decree of] Allah came upon them from where they had not expected, and He cast terror into their hearts.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes a tribe whose strongholds failed because defeat came from a direction they did not expect and their courage collapsed.
islam.tie_back: It shows why the Kural requires a fort that cannot be taken in any way, including from an unexpected direction or by a collapse inside.
islam._accuracy_note: A theological lesson about trusting in forts, which the Kural does not share. The overlap is the collapse from within.

judaism.quote_or_event: “One wise man prevailed over a city of warriors and brought down its mighty stronghold.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs observes that one clever strategist can bring down a stronghold that force could not.
judaism.tie_back: It names the danger in the Kural’s third method: stratagem, which a true fort must be proof against.
judaism._accuracy_note: The proverb praises wisdom; the Kural requires resistance to it, so the parallel is the reverse side of the same idea.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Furthermore, the royal frontier fortress has a gate-keeper — wise, experienced, intelligent — to keep out those he doesn’t know and to let in those he does.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha’s fortress has a wise gatekeeper who admits only people he knows.
buddhism.tie_back: The gatekeeper guards against the Kural’s third danger, infiltration and treachery.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 7.63, Nagara Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good match on protection against infiltration; the sutta also says the fort resists ‘duplicitous allies’.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After ten years in which neither siege nor battle could take Troy, the Greeks left the wooden horse, filled with hidden warriors, outside the walls. The Trojans drew it into the city themselves, and the men inside opened the gates.
greek_mythology.explanation: Troy withstood blockade and assault but fell to a trick that got enemies inside the walls.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Troy passed the Kural’s first two tests and failed the third: it was taken by deceit.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; a classic example of the Kural’s three methods of capture.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The rule is, not to besiege walled cities if it can possibly be avoided.”
philosophy.explanation: Sun Tzu advises against attacking walled cities directly because sieges cost so much.
philosophy.tie_back: The strategist’s rule assumes the Kural’s fort: one so hard to take by siege or storm that attackers should avoid it.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War 3.4 (trans. Lionel Giles)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Matches the difficulty of siege; Sun Tzu elsewhere relies on spies, the Kural’s third threat.

kurals.tamil:
முற்றாற்றி முற்றி யவரையும் பற்றாற்றிப்
பற்றியார் வெல்வது அரண்.
kurals.transliteration:
Mutraatri mutri yavaraiyum patraatrip
patriyaar velvathu aran.
kurals.meaning: A true fortress lets those inside, holding firm to their positions, defeat even a strong army skilled at siegecraft that surrounds them.
kurals.elementary: In a game of king-of-the-hill, the one on top can hold off a crowd of climbers as long as he keeps his footing. Valluvar says a good fort works like that hill. Even when many skilled attackers surround it, the defenders who hold their ground can win.
kurals.university: The couplet repeats two roots in a tight pattern. Mutraatri mutriyavar means ‘those who besiege, being skilled (aatri) in besieging’, i.e. an expert siege force, and patraatrip patriyaar means ‘those who hold on, being able to hold (their ground)’, i.e. the defenders who do not let go of the place they occupy. Varadarasanar reads patru as the defenders’ attachment to their position, and Pappaiah as not abandoning their post. The fort is defined by its result: it is that in which the holders defeat (velvathu) even a skilled besieger. The repeated sounds (mutru, patru) make the couplet memorable. It shifts the chapter from the fort’s structure to the fort in action, preparing for 749-750. The sandhi-joined text on thirukkural-thamizh.org is ‘முற்றாற்றி முற்றி யவரையும் பற்றாற்றிப் / பற்றியார் வெல்வ தரண்’, which matches ytamizh.com.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “As enemies do not hurt these (beings, when they are) sheltered by (their) fortresses, even so foes (can) not injure a king who has taken refuge in his fort.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu compares a king in his fort to animals safe in their natural shelters, where enemies cannot harm them.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, Manu promises that those who hold their fort cannot be overcome by those outside.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Stresses safety more than victory over the besiegers.

christianity.quote_or_event: “There was a little city, and few men within it; and there came a great king against it, and besieged it, and built great bulwarks against it: Now there was found in it a poor wise man, and he by his wisdom delivered the city.”
christianity.explanation: The Preacher tells of a small city with few defenders that was saved from a great king’s siege.
christianity.tie_back: It is the Kural’s scene: a few who hold their ground defeating a powerful besieger.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close match on outcome. The city is saved by wisdom rather than by its walls, which also points ahead to 750.

islam.quote_or_event: At the Battle of the Trench (627 CE), the Muslims of Medina dug a trench across the city’s open approach and held their positions against a much larger confederate army. After a long siege, harsh weather and divisions among them led the besiegers to withdraw; the Qur’an recalls the episode in Surat al-Ahzab.
islam.explanation: Defenders who kept their line behind a prepared defense outlasted a stronger besieging force.
islam.tie_back: It is a clear case of the Kural’s holders who, keeping their ground, defeat the besiegers.
islam.source: Qur’an 33:9-25 and the sira accounts of the Battle of the Trench (al-Khandaq)
islam._accuracy_note: Historical paraphrase; the Qur’an credits the victory mainly to God’s help, the wind and unseen forces.

judaism.quote_or_event: The books of Kings, Isaiah and Chronicles tell how Sennacherib of Assyria surrounded Jerusalem in Hezekiah’s day, having already taken the other fortified towns of Judah. Jerusalem did not surrender, and the Assyrian army withdrew without taking the city.
judaism.explanation: Jerusalem, held by its defenders, outlasted the greatest siege army of its age.
judaism.tie_back: It is the Kural’s fort in practice: a skilled besieger defeated by those who held firm inside.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. The biblical text credits deliverance mainly to divine action, not to the defenders.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “then it is said to be a royal frontier fortress that can't be undone by external foes or duplicitous allies.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says that a fully equipped frontier fortress cannot be defeated by enemies outside or false friends inside.
buddhism.tie_back: ‘Can’t be undone’ is the Kural’s fort, which beats even skilled besiegers.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 7.63, Nagara Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Matches on invincibility; the sutta does not describe the defenders winning actively.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: For nine years the Achaean army camped before Troy without taking it; in the Iliad the Trojans, holding the city, even drive the Greeks back to their ships during Achilles’ absence.
greek_mythology.explanation: Troy’s defenders held their walls against the largest army of the heroic age for a decade.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Troy long showed the Kural’s point: defenders who held their ground wore down a mighty besieger.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; Troy eventually fell, so the example fits the long defense only.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Sun Tzu said: The good fighters of old first put themselves beyond the possibility of defeat, and then waited for an opportunity of defeating the enemy.”
philosophy.explanation: Sun Tzu teaches that a commander first makes himself safe from defeat and then waits for the chance to win.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s defenders do the same: they hold firm in their fort and then overcome the besiegers.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War 4.1 (trans. Lionel Giles)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close on the strategy of secure holding followed by victory.

kurals.tamil:
முனைமுகத்து மாற்றலர் சாய வினைமுகத்து
வீறெய்தி மாண்ட தரண்.
kurals.transliteration:
Munaimukaththu maatralar saaya vinaimukaththu
veereythi maanda tharan.
kurals.meaning: A true fortress wins fame through the fighting skill of its defenders, which brings the enemy down at the very front line of battle.
kurals.elementary: A castle becomes famous not just because its walls are pretty but because of the brave defenders who stopped every attack at the gate. People tell stories about what they did there. Valluvar says a fort gets its greatness from the deeds done in its defense.
kurals.university: The couplet sets munaimukam (the battle-front) against vinaimukam (the field of action or operations): the enemy (maatralar) falls (saaya) at the front because of what the defenders do, and through those deeds the fort attains distinction (veeru eythi) and excellence (maanda). Pappaiah notes that the enemy is destroyed ‘as soon as battle begins’, and Kalaignar stresses attacks launched from within. Veeru, ‘pride, distinction, uniqueness’, suggests that a fort’s fame comes from the deeds done in its defense rather than from its stones. The couplet is thus the bridge between the structural couplets (742-747) and the conclusion in 750 that without vinai maatchi (excellence in action) no fort exists at all. The repetition of mukaththu (‘at the face of’) in both halves is a characteristic Kural device. The sandhi-joined text is identical in wording to the ytamizh.com reading.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Considering your specific duty as a kṣatriya, you should know that there is no better engagement for you than fighting on religious principles; and so there is no need for hesitation.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna reminds Arjuna that for a warrior, fighting in a righteous battle is the highest duty.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural gives the fort’s glory to the warriors who fight at the front, and the Gita makes such fighting the warrior’s highest calling.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.31 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Speaks of the warrior’s duty in general; forts are not mentioned.

christianity.quote_or_event: “out of weakness were made strong, waxed valiant in fight, turned to flight the armies of the aliens.”
christianity.explanation: Hebrews praises the heroes of faith who became brave in battle and drove back foreign armies.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it finds honor in defenders whose deeds in battle make the enemy flee.
christianity._accuracy_note: General praise of faithful warriors; no fort is involved.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, Allah loves those who fight in His cause in a row as though they are a [single] structure joined firmly.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises believers who stand together in battle as solidly as a well-built wall.
islam.tie_back: The defenders themselves become the fortification, and their firm stand is what earns honor, as in the Kural.
islam._accuracy_note: Good match on defenders as a fort; the verse speaks of God’s love rather than a fort’s fame.

judaism.quote_or_event: “As for the builders, each had his sword girded at his side as he was building.”
judaism.explanation: Nehemiah’s builders worked on Jerusalem’s wall with swords at their sides, ready to fight.
judaism.tie_back: The wall’s strength came from men ready to act at once, and it is their readiness that the Kural honors.
judaism.source: Nehemiah 4:12 (JPS Tanakh, Gender-Sensitive Edition 2023, via Sefaria; KJV 4:18)
judaism._accuracy_note: Matches readiness for action; no battle is actually fought in the passage.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Realizing that this body is as fragile as a clay pot, and fortifying this mind like a well-fortified city, fight out Mara with the sword of wisdom. Then, guarding the conquest, remain unattached.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells the practitioner to fortify the mind like a city and actively fight Mara from it.
buddhism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the fortified city is a base for active fighting, not just a place to hide.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Spiritual metaphor, but the structure (fortify, then fight from it) matches closely.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad, Hector is the chief defender of Troy: his infant son is called Astyanax, ‘lord of the city’, because Hector alone protected Ilios, and his attacks from the city drive the Greeks back to their ships.
greek_mythology.explanation: Troy’s glory in the epic rests on Hector’s deeds on the battlefield.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hector is the Kural’s idea in a single hero: the city’s fame comes from its defender’s deeds at the front.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “A city will be well fortified which is surrounded by brave men and not by bricks.”
philosophy.explanation: In a saying attributed to Lycurgus, the Spartan lawgiver says that brave men are a better wall than bricks.
philosophy.tie_back: It anticipates the Kural’s conclusion that a fort’s worth lies in its defenders’ deeds.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Life of Lycurgus 19.4 (trans. B. Perrin, LacusCurtius)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Plutarch himself doubts whether the letters containing the saying are authentic. The saying also rejects walls, which the Kural does not.

kurals.tamil:
எனைமாட்சித் தாகியக் கண்ணும் வினைமாட்சி
இல்லார்கண் இல்லது அரண்.
kurals.transliteration:
Enaimaatchith thaakiyak kannum vinaimaatchi
illaarkan illathu aran.
kurals.meaning: However excellent a fortress may be, it is no fortress at all in the hands of people who lack skill and vigor in action.
kurals.elementary: You could have the best football in the world, but if nobody on your team can kick, you will still lose. A fort is the same. The tallest walls are useless if the people inside don’t know how to defend them. Valluvar ends the chapter by saying that people matter more than walls.
kurals.university: The closing couplet undercuts everything before it. Enai maatchiththu aakiya kannum means ‘even when it has every kind of excellence’, summing up the natural defenses, walls, provisions and garrison of 742-749. Yet it is illathu, ‘non-existent’, among those who lack vinai maatchi, excellence in action. Varadarasanar glosses vinai maatchi as skill in the ways of action, Pappaiah as the ability to understand and act against the enemy, and Kalaignar simply says that if those inside are incompetent there is no use at all. The play on maatchi (‘excellence’) in both lines sets the fort’s excellence against its holders’ excellence, and the holders win. Pope’s verse rendering (‘To craven souls no fortress strength supplies’) makes the lack a matter of courage, while the Tamil commentators stress practical competence more broadly. The ytamizh.com Varadarasanar gloss ends with the words ‘பொருள் செயல்வகை’, the title of the next chapter, which appears to be a page artifact rather than part of the commentary. The sandhi-joined text reads ‘எனைமாட்சித் தாகியக் கண்ணும் வினைமாட்சி / யில்லார்க ணில்ல தரண்’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Ramayana, Hanuman reports to Rama that Lanka is guarded by moats, high walls, four great gates and huge numbers of rakshasa troops, making it seem impregnable. Yet the city falls once Ravana, blinded by pride and deaf to good counsel, loses his brother Vibhishana and fights an unrighteous war.
hinduism.explanation: Lanka had every material advantage but was lost because its master lacked wisdom and right action.
hinduism.tie_back: Lanka proves the Kural’s last word: a fort with every excellence is nothing without excellence in those who hold it.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda, Sarga 3 (Hanuman’s description of Lanka) and following

christianity.quote_or_event: “Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it: except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain.”
christianity.explanation: The psalm says walls and watchmen are useless unless God guards the city.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts say the walls themselves are not what protects a city. The psalm points to God, the Kural to capable defenders.
christianity._accuracy_note: Same structure (the fort alone is not enough), but a different answer to what makes it work.

islam.quote_or_event: “They will not fight you all except within fortified cities or from behind walls. Their violence among themselves is severe. You think they are together, but their hearts are diverse.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes enemies who hide behind walls but are divided among themselves, and so are weak despite their fortifications.
islam.tie_back: Walls cannot save a people divided at heart, which is the Kural’s point that a fort is nothing without worthy defenders.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong thematic match on fortified but inwardly weak defenders.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud relates that when Rabbi Yehuda Nesia levied a tax for repairing the city wall even on the Sages, Reish Lakish objected that Torah scholars do not need protection. He cited verses from the Psalms to argue that the merit of the people, not the stones, guards a city.
judaism.explanation: The rabbis ask what really protects a city and put the quality of its people above the wall.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Talmud holds that a wall’s protective power depends on the worth of those within.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. The rabbinic point concerns spiritual merit rather than military competence.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “With persistence as his army, the disciple of the noble ones abandons what is unskillful, develops what is skillful, abandons what is blameworthy, develops what is blameless, and looks after himself with purity.”
buddhism.explanation: In the Nagara Sutta’s application, the fortress’s army stands for the disciple’s own persistent effort.
buddhism.tie_back: The sutta, like the Kural, makes the active effort of those inside what finally decides whether the fortress stands.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 7.63, Nagara Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Allegorical; the match is to the principle that vigorous action inside is decisive.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad, the Greeks build a great wall and ditch around their ships. While Achilles withdraws from battle and the other leading Greek heroes are wounded, Hector breaks the gate with a stone and the Trojans pour over the wall.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Greeks’ fortification failed as soon as its best fighters were missing.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is the Kural’s conclusion in story form: a strong wall is nothing without worthy men to hold it.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For men, and not walls or ships in which are no men, constitute a state.”
philosophy.explanation: The Athenian general Nicias tells his defeated army in Sicily that the city is its people, not its walls.
philosophy.tie_back: This is almost exactly the Kural’s closing verdict: without capable people, walls count for nothing.
philosophy.source: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War 7.77 (trans. Benjamin Jowett, Perseus Digital Library)
